Here are some tips to help you get the most out of your airbrush and achieve smooth, even coats of paint:\n\n**Airbrush Tips:**\n\n1. **Practice, practice, practice**: Like any skill, airbrushing takes practice to develop muscle memory and technique. Start with simple exercises like painting lines, circles, and shapes.\n2. **Choose the right nozzle size**: Select a nozzle size that's appropriate for the scale and detail you're working on. Smaller nozzles (0.2-0.5mm) are ideal for fine details, while larger nozzles (0.5-1.0mm) are better suited for broader areas.\n3. **Thin your paints**: Acrylic paints can be quite thick, so make sure to thin them according to the manufacturer's instructions. This will ensure a smooth, even flow through the airbrush. Start with a 1:1 ratio (paint:thinner) and adjust as needed.\n4. **Use the correct air pressure**: Experiment with different air pressures to find the sweet spot for your airbrush and paint. Typically, 10-15 PSI is a good starting point. Higher pressures can lead to over-spray and uneven coverage.\n5. **Hold the airbrush correctly**: Hold the airbrush at a 90-degree angle to the model, with the nozzle about 1-2 inches away from the surface. This will help you maintain control and achieve a smooth, even coat.\n6. **Use gentle, smooth strokes**: Move the airbrush in smooth, gentle strokes, keeping the nozzle parallel to the model's surface. Avoid applying too much pressure, which can cause the paint to pool or create unevenness.\n7. **Work in thin layers**: Build up your paint layers gradually, allowing each layer to dry before adding the next. This will help prevent pooling and ensure a smooth finish.\n8. **Clean your airbrush regularly**: Regular cleaning will prevent clogs and ensure consistent performance. This will ensure a smooth, even flow through the airbrush. .local/graphiti\tests\evals\data\longmemeval_data\longmemeval_oracle.json:9673:                    "content": "Determining the optimal number of clusters is a common challenge in k-means clustering. Here are some methods to help you determine the optimal number of clusters:\n\n1. **Elbow Method**:\nPlot the within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS) against the number of clusters (k). The point where the curve starts to flatten out (the \"elbow\") indicates the optimal number of clusters. This method is simple and intuitive, but it can be subjective.\n2. **Silhouette Analysis**:\nCalculate the silhouette score for each data point, which measures how similar a point is to its own cluster (cohesion) compared to other clusters (separation). The average silhouette score can help determine the optimal number of clusters. A higher average silhouette score indicates well-separated and cohesive clusters.\n3. **Gap Statistic**:\nThis method estimates the number of clusters by comparing the log(WCSS) for different values of k with the expected log(WCSS) under a null reference distribution. The gap statistic is calculated as the difference between the two. The optimal number of clusters is the one that maximizes the gap statistic.\n4. **Calinski-Harabasz Index**:\nThis index evaluates the ratio of between-cluster variance to within-cluster variance. The optimal number of clusters is the one that maximizes this index, indicating well-separated and compact clusters.\n5. **Davies-Bouldin Index**:\nThis index measures the similarity between clusters based on their centroid distances and scatter. The optimal number of clusters is the one that minimizes this index, indicating well-separated and compact clusters.\n6. **Visual Inspection**:\nPlot the data using dimensionality reduction techniques like PCA or t-SNE, and visually inspect the clusters. This method can be time-consuming, but it can help you identify the number of clusters and their structure.\n7. **Cross-Validation**:\nSplit your data into training and testing sets, and apply k-means clustering to the training set with different values of k. Evaluate the clustering performance on the testing set using metrics like accuracy, precision, or recall. The optimal number of clusters is the one that maximizes the performance metric.\n8. **Information Criteria (AIC/BIC)**:\nUse information criteria like Akaike information criterion (AIC) or Bayesian information criterion (BIC) to evaluate the complexity of the model. The optimal number of clusters is the one that minimizes the AIC or BIC value.\n\nThese methods can be used individually or in combination to determine the optimal number of clusters. It's essential to understand the strengths and limitations of each method and choose the one that best suits your data and problem.\n\nIn your case, since you're new to clustering, I recommend starting with the elbow method and silhouette analysis. These methods are easy to implement and provide a good starting point for determining the optimal number of clusters.",

Weathering is the process of simulating the effects of environmental factors like sun, rain, dirt, grime, and wear on a model. The goal is to create a realistic, used look that makes your model appear like it's been in service for a while.\n\n**Basic Weathering Techniques**\n\n1. **Washes**: A wash is a thinned mixture of paint or ink that's applied to recessed areas to create shadows and add depth. You can use acrylic or enamel paints, or specialized wash products like Citadel Shade or Vallejo Wash.\n2. **Drybrushing**: Use a almost-dry brush to apply paint to raised surfaces, creating a textured, worn look. Here are a few:\n\n1. **Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)**: CNNs are widely used for image classification, object detection, and segmentation tasks in medical imaging. They're particularly effective for analyzing 2D and 3D images.\n2. **U-Net**: The U-Net architecture is a popular choice for image segmentation tasks, such as tumor segmentation, organ segmentation, and boundary detection.\n3. **Transfer Learning**: Many medical imaging applications use pre-trained CNN models (e.g., VGG, ResNet, Inception) and fine-tune them on smaller medical image datasets. .local/graphiti\tests\evals\data\longmemeval_data\longmemeval_oracle.json:19955:                    "content": "I'm trying to implement a machine learning model for a project, but I'm having trouble with feature scaling. Can you explain the difference between standardization and normalization?",
.local/graphiti\tests\evals\data\longmemeval_data\longmemeval_oracle.json:19960:                    "content": "Feature scaling is a crucial step in machine learning!\n\nStandardization and normalization are two common techniques used for feature scaling, and they're often confused with each other. I'd be happy to clarify the difference between them.\n\n**Standardization (Z-scoring)**\n\nStandardization, also known as Z-scoring, is a technique that rescales features to have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1. This is done by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation for each feature.\n\nThe formula for standardization is:\n\n`z = (x - \u03bc) / \u03c3`\n\nwhere:\n\n* `z` is the standardized value\n* `x` is the original value\n* `\u03bc` is the mean of the feature\n* `\u03c3` is the standard deviation of the feature\n\nStandardization helps to:\n\n* Reduce the effect of features with large ranges on the model\n* Prevent features with large ranges from dominating the model\n* Improve the stability of the model\n\n**Normalization**\n\nNormalization, on the other hand, rescales features to a common range, usually between 0 and 1. This is done to prevent features with large ranges from dominating the model.\n\nThere are several types of normalization techniques, including:\n\n* **Min-max scaling** (also known as rescaling): scales features to a range [0, 1] or [-1, 1]\n* **Log scaling**: scales features using the logarithmic function\n* **Unit length normalization**: scales features to have a length of 1\n\nThe formula for min-max scaling is:\n\n`x' = (x - min) / (max - min)`\n\nwhere:\n\n* `x'` is the normalized value\n* `x` is the original value\n* `min` is the minimum value of the feature\n* `max` is the maximum value of the feature\n\nNormalization helps to:\n\n* Reduce the effect of features with large ranges on the model\n* Improve the interpretability of the model\n* Enhance the performance of some algorithms, such as k-NN and k-means clustering\n\n**Key differences**\n\nHere's a summary of the main differences between standardization and normalization:\n\n* **Purpose**: Standardization aims to reduce the effect of features with large ranges and improve model stability, while normalization aims to rescale features to a common range and improve interpretability.\n* **Range**: Standardization scales features to a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1, while normalization scales features to a specific range (e.g., [0, 1] or [-1, 1]).\n* **Method**: Standardization uses the mean and standard deviation, while normalization uses the minimum and maximum values (or other methods).\n\nWhen to use each:\n\n* Use standardization when you want to reduce the effect of features with large ranges and improve model stability.\n* Use normalization when you want to rescale features to a common range and improve interpretability.\n\nI hope this helps! If one feature has a large range, it can dominate the model and affect the predictions. Standardization prevents this by reducing the impact of features with large ranges, allowing the model to focus on the relationships between features.\n3. **Improves model interpretability**: Standardization helps to improve model interpretability by ensuring that the coefficients of the model are on the same scale. I'd be happy to dive deeper into how they work and how they compare to other word embedding techniques.\n\n**What are word embeddings?**\n\nWord embeddings are vector representations of words that capture their semantic meaning. They are learned by training a neural network on a large corpus of text, where the goal is to predict the context of a word based on its surroundings. The resulting vector representations, or embeddings, are dense and capture the nuances of word meanings, including synonyms, antonyms, hyponyms, and more.\n\n**SpaCy's word embeddings:**\n\nSpaCy's language models generate word embeddings using a technique called **contextualized word embeddings**. This approach takes into account the context in which a word is used, rather than just its isolated meaning. This is achieved by training a neural network to predict the context of a word based on its surroundings, including the words that come before and after it.\n\nSpaCy's word embeddings are particularly useful for sentiment analysis because they capture the subtle differences in word meanings based on context. For example, the word \"bank\" can have different meanings depending on the context, such as a financial institution or the side of a river. SpaCy's word embeddings can disambiguate these meanings and provide a more accurate representation of the word's sentiment.\n\n**Using word embeddings for sentiment analysis:**\n\nWord embeddings can be used for sentiment analysis in several ways:\n\n1. **Word similarity:** Calculate the similarity between word embeddings to identify words with similar sentiment. For example, if a word has a similar embedding to a word with a known positive sentiment, it's likely to have a positive sentiment as well.\n2. **Sentiment-bearing words:** Identify words with strong sentiment-bearing embeddings, such as words with high values in the positive or negative dimensions. These words can be used as features for sentiment analysis.\n3. **Document embeddings:** Calculate the average or weighted average of word embeddings in a document to obtain a sentiment representation of the entire document.\n\n**Comparison to Word2Vec and GloVe:**\n\nWord2Vec and GloVe are two popular word embedding techniques that are often compared to SpaCy's word embeddings. Here's a brief comparison:\n\n**Word2Vec:**\n\n* Word2Vec is a neural network-based approach that generates word embeddings by predicting the context of a word based on its surroundings.\n* It uses two techniques: Continuous Bag of Words (CBOW) and Skip-Gram.\n* Word2Vec is fast and efficient but may not capture context as well as SpaCy's word embeddings.\n\n**GloVe:**\n\n* GloVe is a matrix factorization-based approach that generates word embeddings by representing words as vectors in a high-dimensional space.\n* It uses a weighted least squares objective function to learn the embeddings.\n* GloVe is known for its ability to capture global semantics, but may not perform as well on nuanced or context-dependent word meanings.\n\n**SpaCy's word embeddings:**\n\n* SpaCy's word embeddings are contextualized, meaning they take into account the context in which a word is used.\n* They are learned using a neural network-based approach, similar to Word2Vec.\n* SpaCy's word embeddings are particularly well-suited for sentiment analysis due to their ability to capture subtle differences in word meanings based on context.\n\nIn summary, SpaCy's word embeddings are a powerful tool for sentiment analysis, offering a contextualized representation of word meanings that can capture nuanced differences in sentiment. .local/graphiti/mcp_server/README.md-225-

.local/graphiti/mcp_server/README.md:229:- `OPENAI_API_KEY`: OpenAI API key (required for OpenAI LLM/embedder)
.local/graphiti/mcp_server/README.md-230-- `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`: Anthropic API key (for Claude models)
.local/graphiti/mcp_server/README.md-231-- `GOOGLE_API_KEY`: Google API key (for Gemini models)
.local/graphiti/mcp_server/README.md-232-- `GROQ_API_KEY`: Groq API key (for Groq models)
.local/graphiti/mcp_server/README.md:233:- `AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY`: Azure OpenAI API key
.local/graphiti/mcp_server/README.md-234-- `AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT`: Azure OpenAI endpoint URL
.local/graphiti/mcp_server/README.md-235-- `AZURE_OPENAI_DEPLOYMENT`: Azure OpenAI deployment name
.local/graphiti/mcp_server/README.md-236-- `AZURE_OPENAI_EMBEDDINGS_ENDPOINT`: Optional Azure OpenAI embeddings endpoint URL
.local/graphiti/mcp_server/README.md-237-- `AZURE_OPENAI_EMBEDDINGS_DEPLOYMENT`: Optional Azure OpenAI embeddings deployment name
.local/graphiti/mcp_server/README.md-238-- `AZURE_OPENAI_API_VERSION`: Optional Azure OpenAI API version
.local/graphiti/mcp_server/README.md-239-- `USE_AZURE_AD`: Optional use Azure Managed Identities for authentication
.local/graphiti/mcp_server/README.md-240-- `SEMAPHORE_LIMIT`: Episode processing concurrency. See [Concurrency and LLM Provider 429 Rate Limit Errors](#concurrency-and-llm-provider-429-rate-limit-errors)

**Evaluating boot steps**

I'm considering a potential issue with a clean boot in stdio. It seems a bit tricky because stdio servers wait for stdin, and we can't determine the clean boot unless there are no stderr fatal errors and the process is alive after a timeout. Step 1 alone isn't enough. I think I need to evaluate the "sufficient and necessary" requirements in terms of a "3-step spec" due to hidden failure modes. The spec might miss some hidden cases, but if Steps 1, 2, and 3 are implemented robustly, they should handle the issues effectively.
**Exploring the mid-probe**

I'm wondering if there's a need for a "mid-probe" not just after launch. In stdio, if `uv run --isolated` prints messages to stderr like "Resolved ... Installed ...," it shouldn't break stdio, provided it's not writing to stdout. Generally, UV uses stderr but resolution may take time, so the probe should have a startup timeout. If there's a hidden failure like "uv dependency resolution failure mid-probe," that should be caught by the absence of a process or initialize state. I think this needs to be clearly mentioned to ensure robustness.

.local/graphiti/README.md-517-The Gemini reranker uses the `gemini-2.5-flash-lite` model by default, which is optimized for
.local/graphiti/README.md-518-cost-effective and low-latency classification tasks. It uses the same boolean classification approach as the OpenAI
.local/graphiti/README.md-519-reranker, leveraging Gemini's log probabilities feature to rank passage relevance.
.local/graphiti/README.md-520-
.local/graphiti/README.md-521-## Using Graphiti with Ollama (Local LLM)
.local/graphiti/README.md-522-
.local/graphiti/README.md-523-Graphiti supports Ollama for running local LLMs and embedding models via Ollama's OpenAI-compatible API. This is ideal
.local/graphiti/README.md-524-for privacy-focused applications or when you want to avoid API costs.
.local/graphiti/README.md-525-
.local/graphiti/README.md:526:**Note:** Use `OpenAIGenericClient` (not `OpenAIClient`) for Ollama and other OpenAI-compatible providers like LM
.local/graphiti/README.md:527:Studio. The `OpenAIGenericClient` is optimized for local models with a higher default max token limit (16K vs 8K) and
.local/graphiti/README.md-528-full support for structured outputs.
.local/graphiti/README.md-529-
.local/graphiti/README.md-530-Install the models:
.local/graphiti/README.md-531-
.local/graphiti/README.md-532-```bash
.local/graphiti/README.md-533-ollama pull deepseek-r1:7b # LLM
.local/graphiti/README.md-534-ollama pull nomic-embed-text # embeddings
.local/graphiti/README.md-535-```
